messages.body_plain:
You should increase the value of step. This argument indicates the distance between pseudomarkers and so the density of positions at which you are doing calculations. If the number of markers are different, presumably the chromosome lengths are somewhat different and so the number of markers and pseudomarkers you end up with will be different.

The appropriate value of step depends on the number of individuals and the type of cross, but I'm not aware of a case where you'd have mapping resolution to 0.001 cM, and seldom do you get precision < 1 cM, so I typically am using step=1 and occasionally like step=0.2. But step=0.2 usually in a targeted way, for example when I'm trying to get more precise endpoints for a LOD support interval.

karl

Hi,
We have one population consisted of 192 F3 lines resulting from a cross between two plant genomes.

I ran Genotype-Corrector ( https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-28294-0 ) which lead to 7065 markers. It had an option to output the results in R/QTL (please see attached). Below are the commands and in order to be able to use F3 I had to specify it as RIL:

python -m schnablelab.imputation.GC qc_sd gc-missing.map gc-sdtest.map --population RIL --sig_cutoff 0.0001

python -m schnablelab.imputation.GC format gc-final.map --rqtl --pop_type RIL

Loading the output into R\QTL it has given me that I use F2:

> library(qtl)
> mycross <- read.cross(format="csv", dir="~/data/", file="gc-final.rqtl.csv" )
 --Read the following data:
	 7064  individuals
	 192  markers
	 1  phenotypes
 --Cross type: f2

How do I change it to F3 or RIL?

Thank you in advance,

Best wishes,

Michal

messages.body_plain:
The plot of LOD score vs estimated recombination fraction for all marker pairs can reveal certain problems, like whether markers have their alleles switched. But it looks fine in your case. Marker pairs that are truly unlinked will have estimated rec frac that varies a bit +/- 0.5, with low LOD score, and that’s what you’re seeing.

To figure out marker order, I would first look at at plot of the pairwise rec fracs for a particular chromosome, or for pairs of chromosomes. (All chromosomes won’t be feasible given the large number of markers you have.) I’d then study large gaps in the estimated genetic map.

(Sometimes I accidentally reply to the individual rather than to the list; probably I did that in this case.)

karl

The "csv" format is working.

The "benth_gc-final.rqtl.csv" file has markers as columns and lines as rows, so read.cross with format="csvr" gives an error, but format="csv" works.

Your first line

   mycross <- read.cross(format="csvr", ....)

gives the error "you must include at least one phenotype"

But then the next call summary(mycross) works, though with a warning, because apparently you'd previously read in the data using format="csv", since the mycross object exists.

The warning message you're getting about "Some chromosomes > 1000 cM ..." is because your data  file doesn't have a map, and so it plugs in an arbitrary map, which ends up being really long because there are >10,000 markers.

karl

messages.body_plain:
The hyper data are included with R/qtl, in its internal format:

   library(qtl)
   data(hyper)
   ls()

We don't have a CSV file available, but you could write it to a file
with write.cross():

   write.cross(hyper, "csv", "hyper")

this will create a file "hyper.csv" in your R working directory.

karl

Hi folks:

Does anyone know if the 2-part model in scanone will run for a 4-way mapping population design?
Best,
Tom
messages.body_snippet:
Hi folks:

Does anyone know if the 2-part model in scanone will run for a 4-way mapping population design?
Best,
Tom

messages.subject: Re: 2-part model
messages.subject_clean: 2-part model
messages.body_plain:
Yes it seems to work. Here's an example:

    library(qtl)
    data(fake.4way)
    fake.4way <- calc.genoprob(fake.4way, step=1)
    fake.4way$pheno[fake.4way$pheno[,1] < 6, 1] <- 0
    out <- scanone(fake.4way, model="2part")
    plot(out, lod=1:3)

karl
